concept.name: Broadening formation
concept.definition: A classical technical-analysis pattern in which successively higher highs and lower lows produce two diverging trend lines, so the trading range widens over time — the opposite of a triangle. Occurring more often at tops (where it is conventionally assigned bearish implications), it is read as a market out of control, with public speculation replacing informed participation. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Each swing overshoots the last in both directions — buyers chase new highs and then panic to new lows — a signature of emotional, leaderless trading rather than orderly accumulation or distribution.
concept.mechanics: Require five minor reversals (three successively higher peaks and two lower troughs, or vice versa), with volume irregular and offering no directional clue. The bearish reading is confirmed only when price breaks below the lower of the two declining troughs and keeps falling. There is no standard measured target; the widening swings themselves define the pattern.
concept.failure_modes: Because every swing breaks a prior extreme, breakout traders are repeatedly whipsawed in both directions; the 'confirmation' breakdown can itself be just another widening swing that reverses into a new high. Trend-line placement is unusually subjective given the expanding range.
concept.misconceptions: That broadening formations are common, reliable topping signals — they are comparatively rare, and the widening structure resolves in either direction often enough that it is best treated as a warning of instability, not a short signal by itself.
concept.example: A stock in a late-stage rally peaks at $50, dips to $44, rallies to $53, falls to $41, and spikes to $56 on chaotic volume; when price then breaks decisively below $41, the broadening top is considered confirmed.
